claim: The Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas (ADMBA) contains data for eight mouse brains at different developmental stages: E11.5, E13.5, E15.5, E18.5, P4, P14, P28, and P56.
source: The ADMBA contains data for eight mouse brains, each at a different development stage: embryonic day (E)11.5, E13.5, E15.5, E18.5, postnatal day (P) 4, P14, P28, and P56.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the manuscript describing the composition of the ADMBA dataset.

claim: The ADMBA data are generated from 158 to 456 serial 2D sagittal sections of 20–25 µm stained with Nissl or Feulgen-HP yellow.
source: The data are generated from 158 to 456 serial 2D sagittal sections of 20–25 µm stained with Nissl or Feulgen-HP yellow and imaged with a light microscope at a lateral resolution of 0.99 to 1.049 µm.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the ADMBA data generation process.

claim: For the three earliest developmental stages (E11.5, E13.5, E15.5), the entire embryo was imaged rather than just the brain.
source: For the three earliest stages of development, E11.5, E13.5, E15.5, the entire embryo was imaged, rather than just the brain.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the imaging scope for early developmental stages.

claim: Only sections on the left side of each brain are annotated in the ADMBA.
source: Viewed sagittally, these labels cover the majority of tissue in each brain with smooth, anatomically aligned edges (Figure 2A); however, only sections on the left side of each brain are annotated and, for six atlases, labels are not present for the most lateral 14–24% sagittal planes of the brain (4–5% by volume; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes a limitation of the original ADMBA annotations.

claim: For six atlases in the ADMBA, labels are not present for the most lateral 14–24% sagittal planes of the brain (4–5% by volume).
source: Viewed sagittally, these labels cover the majority of tissue in each brain with smooth, anatomically aligned edges (Figure 2A); however, only sections on the left side of each brain are annotated and, for six atlases, labels are not present for the most lateral 14–24% sagittal planes of the brain (4–5% by volume; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 2B).
evidence: This quantifies the extent of missing labels in the original ADMBA.

claim: The median label to atlas volume ratio in the original ADMBA is 51%.
source: Labels extend slightly beyond the midline for several atlases, helping to annotate brains with a midline skew, yielding a median label to atlas volume ratio of 51%.
evidence: This provides a quantitative measure of label coverage in the original atlases.

claim: The Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) for the original labels in the annotated hemisphere ranged from 0.85 to 0.97 with a median of 0.91.
source: The observed DSCs for the original labels in the annotated hemisphere ranged from 0.85 to 0.97 (median 0.91; Figure 2).
evidence: This quantifies the similarity between microscopy images and original label annotations.

claim: After lateral edge extension, the DSC between microscopy images and labels for the left hemisphere showed a median improvement of 0.02 (p=0.02, WSRT).
source: Recalculating the DSC between the microscopy images and labels for the left hemisphere showed greater similarity across all eight atlases with a median DSC improvement of 0.02 (p=0.02, WSRT) and a resulting DSC range of 0.87 to 0.97 (median 0.93, Figure 2D).
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in label accuracy after the extension process.

claim: The original ADMBA atlases have high-frequency artifacts along most edge borders in axial and coronal planes.
source: Visual inspection of labels in the axial and coronal planes reveals high-frequency artifacts along most edge borders, likely from the difficulty of drawing contiguous borders in dimensions orthogonal to the drawing plane (Figure 1, Figure 3).
evidence: This describes a visual observation of artifacts in the original atlases.

claim: The median compactness of labels in the original ADMBA was 13,343 (mean: 34,099, SD: 44,988).
source: Measuring the compactness of each label and taking the weighted mean based on label volume for each atlas gave a median compactness of 13,343 (mean: 34,099, standard deviation (SD): 44,988).
evidence: This provides a quantitative measure of label smoothness in the original atlases.

claim: The thresholded 3D whole-brain microscopy images were more compact than the original labels (median compactness: 1895, mean: 2615, SD: 2305; p=0.02, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected).
source: For context, across all eight atlases the thresholded 3D whole-brain microscopy images were more compact (median compactness: 1895, mean: 2615, SD: 2305; p=0.02, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected for three comparisons; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), consistent with the observed irregularity in the label images compared to anatomical images (Figure 2B and Figure 3).
evidence: This provides a comparison baseline for label compactness.

claim: Using Gaussian smoothing with sigma 0.25, the median atlas-wide smoothing quality across all eight atlases was 0.54 (mean 0.53).
source: At this sigma value, the median atlas-wide smoothing quality across all eight atlases was 0.54 (mean 0.53), rising to a peak of 0.57 (mean 0.56) at sigma 0.5 and 0.49 (mean 0.53) at a sigma of 1.0, but with substantial loss of labels (median 14% lost at sigma 0.25, rising to 42% lost at sigma 1; mean 11% and 47%, respectively Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This quantifies the performance of Gaussian smoothing approach.

claim: Gaussian smoothing resulted in label loss in all ADMBA atlases, even with a small sigma where labels remained visibly jagged.
source: Assessing the quality of smoothing using Gaussian blur with increasing Gaussian sigmas, we observed label loss in all atlases in the ADMBA, even with a small sigma where labels remained visibly jagged.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the Gaussian smoothing approach.

claim: The adaptive opening filter approach achieved a median atlas-wide smoothing quality of 0.61 (mean 0.62) across all eight atlases.
source: Quantifying the improvement with the adaptive opening filter approach, using only filter sizes that completely eliminated label loss, we obtained a median atlas-wide smoothing quality of 0.61 (mean 0.62) across all eight atlases, and improvement over the Gaussian filter approach (sigma 0.25; p=0.008; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This quantifies the performance of the proposed adaptive opening filter method.

claim: The adaptive opening filter approach showed significant improvement over Gaussian smoothing (p=0.008, WSRT).
source: Quantifying the improvement with the adaptive opening filter approach, using only filter sizes that completely eliminated label loss, we obtained a median atlas-wide smoothing quality of 0.61 (mean 0.62) across all eight atlases, and improvement over the Gaussian filter approach (sigma 0.25; p=0.008; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This provides statistical evidence for the superiority of the adaptive opening filter.

claim: The optimal filter size for the adaptive opening filter varied between atlases, ranging from 2 to 7.
source: The optimal filter size varied between atlases, ranging from 2 to 7 (E15.5 and P14 shown in Figure 3C,D; all ADMBA shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the variability in optimal parameters across different atlases.

claim: After smoothing, the median overall compactness improved significantly from 13,343 (SD = 44,988) to 2527 (SD = 2634), p=0.02, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected.
source: The median overall compactness improved significantly (13,343 (SD = 44,988) for unsmoothed labels vs. 2527 (SD = 2634) for smoothed labels, p=0.02, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected for the three comparisons; mean 34,099 vs. 3172) to a level that did not differ from that observed for the microscopy images of whole brains (p=1.00, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected for the three comparisons; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in label smoothness after the adaptive opening filter.

claim: After smoothing, label compactness did not differ significantly from that of microscopy images of whole brains (p=1.00, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected).
source: The median overall compactness improved significantly (13,343 (SD = 44,988) for unsmoothed labels vs. 2527 (SD = 2634) for smoothed labels, p=0.02, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected for the three comparisons; mean 34,099 vs. 3172) to a level that did not differ from that observed for the microscopy images of whole brains (p=1.00, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected for the three comparisons; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This demonstrates that the smoothed labels achieved biological-level compactness.

claim: Edge-aware reannotation and smoothing led to a significant reduction in edge distances from a median of 187 million to 86 million µm (p=0.008, WSRT).
source: To quantify this improvement brain-wide, we calculated the sum of edge distances for each pixel at label surfaces across the ADMBA. We observed a significant reduction from a median of 187 million to 86 million µm (p=0.008, WSRT; Figure 4B,C,F), with a median Dice Similarity Coefficient between original (mirrored) and smoothed (edge-aware) labels of 0.76 (mean 0.80) and 9% median (mean 12%) volume reassignment.
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in anatomical alignment after edge-aware processing.

claim: The median Dice Similarity Coefficient between original (mirrored) and smoothed (edge-aware) labels was 0.76 (mean 0.80).
source: To quantify this improvement brain-wide, we calculated the sum of edge distances for each pixel at label surfaces across the ADMBA. We observed a significant reduction from a median of 187 million to 86 million µm (p=0.008, WSRT; Figure 4B,C,F), with a median Dice Similarity Coefficient between original (mirrored) and smoothed (edge-aware) labels of 0.76 (mean 0.80) and 9% median (mean 12%) volume reassignment.
evidence: This quantifies the similarity between original and refined labels.

claim: Edge-aware labeling resulted in 9% median (mean 12%) volume reassignment.
source: To quantify this improvement brain-wide, we calculated the sum of edge distances for each pixel at label surfaces across the ADMBA. We observed a significant reduction from a median of 187 million to 86 million µm (p=0.008, WSRT; Figure 4B,C,F), with a median Dice Similarity Coefficient between original (mirrored) and smoothed (edge-aware) labels of 0.76 (mean 0.80) and 9% median (mean 12%) volume reassignment.
evidence: This quantifies the extent of label boundary changes after refinement.

claim: Edge-aware labeling significantly decreased the coefficient of variation of intensity values within labels from a median of 0.290 to 0.282 (p=0.008, WSRT).
source: We used the coefficient of variation of intensity values within each label to quantify this expectation and demonstrated significantly lower variation with edge-aware labeling (median from all labels weighted by size decreased from 0.290 to 0.282, p=0.008, for all eight atlases, WSRT; Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in within-label homogeneity after edge-aware processing.

claim: Edge-aware labeling decreased the absolute coefficient of variation for 92 of the 100 individual labels represented by all atlases.
source: Furthermore, edge-aware labeling decreased the absolute coefficient of variation for 92 of the 100 individual labels represented by all atlases.
evidence: This demonstrates the broad applicability of the improvement across labels.

claim: The authors imaged 15 intact whole P0 mouse brains (10 male, 5 female) using tissue clearing and lightsheet microscopy.
source: After clearing C57BL/6J WT mouse pup brains (age P0) with simultaneous incubation in SYTO 16 nuclear dye for 2 weeks, we imaged intact whole brains by lightsheet microscopy at 5x to obtain volumetric images at cellular resolution (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), taking approximately 3 hr to image and generating approximately 500 GB of data per brain (n = 15; 10 male, 5 female).
evidence: This describes the validation dataset generated by the authors.

claim: Lightsheet imaging of a P0 mouse brain took approximately 3 hours and generated approximately 500 GB of data per brain.
source: After clearing C57BL/6J WT mouse pup brains (age P0) with simultaneous incubation in SYTO 16 nuclear dye for 2 weeks, we imaged intact whole brains by lightsheet microscopy at 5x to obtain volumetric images at cellular resolution (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), taking approximately 3 hr to image and generating approximately 500 GB of data per brain (n = 15; 10 male, 5 female).
evidence: This provides technical details about the imaging process.

claim: The nuclei detection model achieved a recall (sensitivity) of 90% and precision (positive predictive value) of 92%.
source: The resulting model achieved a recall (sensitivity) of 90% and precision (positive predictive value) of 92%.
evidence: This quantifies the performance of the automated nuclei detection algorithm.

claim: The nuclei detection model showed high correlation with total lightsheet microscopy intensity levels brain-wide (r > 0.99, p≤1 × 10−16, SRCC for both original and smoothed atlases).
source: Furthermore, the model showed high correlation with total lightsheet microscopy intensity levels brain-wide (r > 0.99, p≤1 × 10−16, Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (SRCC) for both original (mirrored) and smoothed (edge-aware) atlases) and nuclei vs. intensity densities (original: r = 0.89; smoothed: r = 0.93; p≤1 × 10−16 for both, SRCC), suggesting the performance was accurate outside the narrow target of the truth set (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This demonstrates the validity of the nuclei detection across the whole brain.

claim: The nuclei detection model showed correlation with nuclei vs. intensity densities (original: r = 0.89; smoothed: r = 0.93; p≤1 × 10−16 for both, SRCC).
source: Furthermore, the model showed high correlation with total lightsheet microscopy intensity levels brain-wide (r > 0.99, p≤1 × 10−16, Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (SRCC) for both original (mirrored) and smoothed (edge-aware) atlases) and nuclei vs. intensity densities (original: r = 0.89; smoothed: r = 0.93; p≤1 × 10−16 for both, SRCC), suggesting the performance was accurate outside the narrow target of the truth set (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This further validates the nuclei detection performance.

claim: The median DSC between registered atlas volumetric histology images and lightsheet microscopy images of each sample brain was 0.91 (mean: 0.91; 95% CI: 0.90–0.92).
source: After registration, the median DSC between the registered atlas volumetric histology images and the lightsheet microscopy images of each sample brain was 0.91 (mean: 0.91; 95% confidence interval: 0.90–0.92; Figure 6—figure supplement 3), although inspection of registered brains also revealed slight misalignments with the atlas, mostly in caudal regions including the cerebellum, a structure known to be challenging for registration (Nazib et al., 2018).
evidence: This quantifies the quality of atlas registration to sample brains.

claim: Edge distances significantly improved for almost all labels with the refined atlas (overall decrease from a median of 153 million µm to 96 million µm, p=0.007, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected).
source: Edge distances significantly improved for almost all labels (overall decrease from a median of 153 million µm to 96 million µm, p=0.007, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected for all 120 labels across all hierarchical levels, mean 152 million to 99 million µm; Figure 7A,C–D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in anatomical alignment in the validation dataset.

claim: The intensity coefficient of variation at the whole-brain level decreased significantly from 0.309 to 0.301 (p=0.007, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected).
source: We observed a small, but significant decrease in the intensity coefficient of variation at the whole-brain level (0.309 to 0.301, p=0.007, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected for the 120 comparisons, mean 0.311 to 0.304) and most sub-labels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in within-label homogeneity in the validation dataset.

claim: For 22 labels (18% of all labels), the variability worsened, but this was only significant (p=0.04) for a single label.
source: For 22 labels (18% of all labels) the variability worsened, however this was only significant (p=0.04) for a single label.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations in the improvement for certain labels.

claim: Variability improved for 98 labels (82% of all labels) with 27 labels showing significant improvement.
source: For context, variability improved for 98 labels (82% of all labels) with 27 labels showing significant improvement.
evidence: This demonstrates the broad applicability of the improvement across most labels.

claim: The coefficient of variation for nuclei density improved significantly overall from a median of 0.629 to 0.625 (p=0.007, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected).
source: We therefore assessed the coefficient of variation for nuclei density and observed a small, but significant improvement with the refined labels overall (median 0.629–0.625, p=0.007, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected for the 120 hierarchical labels, mean 0.629–0.625) and across the majority of labels in the hierarchy (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This quantifies the improvement in nuclei density homogeneity within labels.

claim: A median of 13.5% (4.7 million) nuclei (mean 13.2% [4.6 million] nuclei) were reassigned from original to refined labels.
source: A median of 13.5% (4.7 million) nuclei (mean 13.2% [4.6 million] nuclei) were reassigned from original to refined labels.
evidence: This quantifies the extent of nuclei reassignment after label refinement.

claim: Label refinement reduced isolated, unclustered nuclei by 30% (median 4.4 × 10^5 to 3.1 × 10^5 nuclei; p=0.007, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected).
source: We employed Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) (Ester et al., 1996), an algorithm useful for both clustering and noise or anomaly detection (Ali et al., 2010), and indeed found that label refinement reduced isolated, unclustered nuclei by 30% (median 4.4 × 105 to 3.1 × 105 nuclei; p=0.007, WSRT, Bonferroni corrected for the 120 labels; mean 4.4 × 105 to 3.1 × 105; Figure 7E–F; Figure 7—figure supplement 3), suggesting greater nuclei assignment to labels with nuclei clusters of similar density.
evidence: This demonstrates improved label alignment based on nuclei clustering analysis.

claim: The Allen Common Coordinate Framework atlas (CCFv3) of the adult (P56) C57BL/6J mouse brain represents one of the most complete 3D atlases at microscopic resolution to date.
source: The most recent version of the Allen Common Coordinate Framework atlas (CCFv3) of the adult (P56) C57BL/6J mouse brain represents one of the most complete 3D atlases at microscopic resolution to date (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of existing atlas resources, supported by citation.

claim: The CCFv3 atlas contains 658 structural annotations.
source: A team of neuroanatomists and illustrators redrew structures natively in 3D, sometimes using the original annotations as seeds to guide the redrawing process, producing 658 structural annotations (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the content of the CCFv3 atlas, supported by citation.

claim: 23% of labels from the original Allen Reference Atlas were not included in the CCFv3 3D version, largely due to time and labor constraints.
source: Even with this monumental effort, 23% of labels from the original Allen Reference Atlas were not included in the 3D version, largely due to the time and labor constraints of further manual curation (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes a limitation of the CCFv3 atlas, supported by citation.

claim: Anatomical atlases have played a crucial role in research into organogenesis, anatomy, physiology, and pathology.
source: Anatomical atlases have played a crucial role in research into organogenesis, anatomy, physiology, and pathology (Marquart et al., 2017; Chon et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020) and have been used for a wide range of applications, including investigating developmental biology (Kunst et al., 2019), defining stereotactic coordinates (Franklin and Paxinos, 2013), identifying patterns of neural activity associated with behavior (Renier et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2017), and integrating morphological, transcriptomic, and neural activity data across species (Marquart et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of atlases, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Technological advances in microscopy have facilitated a dramatic increase in imaging of high-resolution, intact whole organs.
source: Technological advances in microscopy have facilitated a dramatic increase in imaging of high-resolution, intact whole organs using serial two-photon tomography (STPT) (Ragan et al., 2012) or tissue clearing techniques (e.g. CLARITY [Chung et al., 2013], 3DISCO [Ertürk et al., 2012], and CUBIC [Susaki et al., 2014]) and lightsheet microscopy (Chhetri et al., 2015; Meijering et al., 2016; Mano et al., 2018; Hillman et al., 2019; Cai et al., 2019; Ueda et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes technological advances in microscopy, supported by multiple citations.

claim: 3D microscopy methods have been applied to map cytoarchitecture and cellular connectivity in complex tissues, including the brain, heart, and lung.
source: These 3D microscopy methods have been applied to map cytoarchitecture and cellular connectivity in complex tissues, including the brain (Cai et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2015; Murakami et al., 2018), heart (Gilbert et al., 2019; Bai et al., 2015), and lung (Li et al., 2012; Ardini-Poleske et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes applications of 3D microscopy, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The progression to 3D microscopy data necessitates 3D anatomical atlases to reference data to existing anatomically-defined labels.
source: The progression to 3D microscopy data necessitates 3D anatomical atlases to reference data to existing anatomically-defined labels (Puelles and Rubenstein, 2003; Watson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the need for 3D atlases, supported by citations.

claim: Most 2D-based atlases suffer from label misalignments or insufficient resolution in the third dimension, limiting their utility for 3D imaging.
source: Although numerous atlases based on 2D physical sections exist (Franklin and Paxinos, 2013; Ardini-Poleske et al., 2017; Savolainen et al., 2009; de Boer et al., 2012; Thompson et al., 2014b), most suffer from label misalignments or insufficient resolution in the third dimension, limiting their utility for 3D imaging (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes limitations of existing 2D atlases, supported by citations.

claim: The Waxholm Space rat brain atlas used two standard reference atlases as templates to yield an atlas with relatively smooth 3D structures through manual and semi-automated segmentation.
source: The Waxholm Space rat brain atlas used two standard reference atlases as templates to yield an atlas with relatively smooth 3D structures through manual and semi-automated segmentation, although some label edge artifacts remain (Papp et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes a prior approach to 3D atlas generation, supported by citation.

claim: Erö et al., 2018 performed non-rigid alignments between histological slice planes of the Common Coordinate Framework (CCFv2, 2011), applying the same deformations to the label images.
source: Erö et al., 2018 performed non-rigid alignments between histological slice planes of the Common Coordinate Framework (CCFv2, 2011), applying the same deformations to the label images.
evidence: This describes another prior approach to atlas refinement, supported by citation.

claim: Niedworok et al., 2016 applied a smoothing filter on the annotations themselves to reduce label artifacts, though many label edge irregularities persisted.
source: Rather than registering planes, Niedworok et al., 2016 applied a smoothing filter on the annotations themselves to reduce label artifacts, though many label edge irregularities persisted.
evidence: This describes yet another prior approach to atlas smoothing, supported by citation.

claim: CUBIC was chosen for tissue clearing given its balance of overall transparency, morphological retention with minimal tissue expansion, and ease of handling as a passive aqueous technique.
source: Among the many available methods to clear whole organs, we chose CUBIC (Susaki et al., 2014; Susaki et al., 2015) given its balance of overall transparency, morphological retention with minimal tissue expansion, and ease of handling as a passive aqueous technique (Kolesová et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2019a; Bossolani et al., 2019).
evidence: This explains the rationale for choosing CUBIC, supported by citations.

claim: The 3D blob detection algorithm using the Laplacian of Gaussian filter has been shown to work well in equivalent image data.
source: To detect nuclei throughout cleared whole brains automatically, we implemented a 3D blob detection algorithm using the Laplacian of Gaussian filter, which has been shown to work well in equivalent image data (Schmid et al., 2010; Figure 6).
evidence: This justifies the choice of detection algorithm, supported by citation.

claim: Elastix has been recently validated as a computationally efficient and accurate tool for registration of mouse brains cleared by CUBIC.
source: Elastix has been recently validated as a computationally efficient and accurate tool for registration of mouse brains cleared by CUBIC (Nazib et al., 2018).
evidence: This justifies the choice of registration tool, supported by citation.

claim: The cerebellum is a structure known to be challenging for registration.
source: After registration, the median DSC between the registered atlas volumetric histology images and the lightsheet microscopy images of each sample brain was 0.91 (mean: 0.91; 95% confidence interval: 0.90–0.92; Figure 6—figure supplement 3), although inspection of registered brains also revealed slight misalignments with the atlas, mostly in caudal regions including the cerebellum, a structure known to be challenging for registration (Nazib et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about registration challenges, supported by citation.

claim: The pipeline extends incomplete labels in each atlas to cover the entire brain and smooth artifacts between 2D sections, whilst respecting anatomical boundaries.
source: Specifically, these tools extended incomplete labels in each atlas to cover the entire brain and smooth artifacts between 2D sections, whilst respecting anatomical boundaries.
evidence: This summarizes the key functions of the proposed pipeline.

claim: The refined labels are more complete, match anatomical images more closely, and have more homogeneous image intensity within labels.
source: We showed that the refined labels are more complete (Figure 2), the interface between labels match anatomical images more closely (Figure 4), and the image intensity within these labels is more homogeneous (Figure 4).
evidence: This summarizes the improvements demonstrated by the authors.

claim: The authors identified the 3D location of 35 million nuclei per brain (median across 15 samples).
source: Using whole-brain lightsheet microscopy of 15 mice at P0, we identified the 3D location of 35 million nuclei per brain (median across 15 samples; Figure 6).
evidence: This quantifies the scale of nuclei detection performed.

claim: The refined labels match anatomical boundaries better at cellular resolution, providing a key step towards comparative analysis of whole-brain cytoarchitecture.
source: We showed that the refined labels match anatomical boundaries better at cellular resolution, providing a key step towards comparative analysis of whole-brain cytoarchitecture (Figure 7).
evidence: This describes the significance of the validation results.

claim: The pipeline is provided as an open source, graphical software suite called MagellanMapper with an end-to-end automated image processing pipeline.
source: Fifth, we have provided the pipeline as an open source, graphical software suite with an end-to-end automated image processing pipeline for refining atlases, detecting nuclei, and quantifying nuclei counts by anatomical label in raw microscopy images of whole tissues.
evidence: This describes the software contribution of the work.

claim: Building a 3D reference atlas from a physically sectioned atlas presents three main challenges: incomplete labels, smoothing jagged edge artifacts, and maintaining anatomical boundaries through the smoothing process.
source: Building a 3D reference atlas from a physically sectioned atlas presents three main challenges: (1) Incomplete labels resulting in unidentified tissues, (2) Smoothing jagged edge artifacts between sections in two of the three dimensions, and (3) Maintaining anatomical boundaries through the smoothing process.
evidence: This summarizes the key challenges addressed by the work.

claim: Prior automated smoothing approaches have well recognized limitations, including labels crossing anatomical boundaries, loss of label detail, and complete loss of small labels.
source: The first is automated smoothing of label boundaries (Niedworok et al., 2016); however, this approach has well recognized limitations (Chen et al., 2019), including labels crossing anatomical boundaries, loss of label detail, and complete loss of small labels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes limitations of prior approaches, supported by citations and data.

claim: The Allen CCFv3 used a combination of novel data generation and copious manual curation by neuroanatomists and illustrators.
source: The second approach uses a combination of novel data generation and copious, manual curation as applied by neuroanatomists and illustrators to version 3 of the Allen Common Coordinate Framework (CCFv3, 2017) (Allen Institute for Brain Science, 2017; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the approach used for the CCFv3 atlas, supported by citations.

claim: The automated method presented is closer to the accuracy of manual curation than prior automated approaches.
source: Our method automates additional curation steps to extend and smooth labels guided by the underlying anatomy, providing an automated method closer to the accuracy of manual curation.
evidence: This is a claim about the relative performance of the proposed method.

claim: Manual curation remains the gold standard for atlas generation.
source: While manual curation remains the gold standard, as performed in the Allen CCFv3, even this monumental effort translated only 77% of labels because of resource limitations (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This acknowledges the superiority of manual curation while noting its limitations.

claim: Future atlas development lies in automated, unbiased approaches.
source: As suggested by Wang et al., future atlas development lies in automated, unbiased approaches (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement supported by citation.

claim: The automated approach creates a foundation for further improvements, substantially reducing the work required to generate a manually curated atlas in the future.
source: Furthermore, it acts as a foundation for further improvements, substantially reducing the work required to generate a manually curated atlas in the future while freeing up anatomists and neuroscientists for the role of oversight in such endeavors.
evidence: This describes the potential impact of the automated approach.

claim: A small number of regions showed a modest increase in variability with the refined labels, most of which were in the hindbrain where histological contrast is lower.
source: While this expectation was correct for the majority of labels (92% of labels present in all atlases), a small number of regions showed a modest increase in variability with our refined labels. Most of these labels were in the hindbrain, where histological contrast is lower, leading to less well-defined anatomical edges.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the approach in certain regions.

claim: Adjusting the weight of edge-detected boundaries based on the degree of underlying intensity contrast could lessen the impact of weak edges on reannotation.
source: Adjusting the weight of edge-detected boundaries, based on the degree of underlying intensity contrast, could lessen the impact of these edges on reannotation.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future improvement.

claim: The use of a single filtering kernel size for smoothing across the entire brain is a limitation.
source: Another limitation is the use of a single filtering kernel size for smoothing across the entire brain (Figure 3).
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the smoothing approach.

claim: In labels with both thick and thin portions, the thin portions are prone to being lost during the erosion step of smoothing.
source: In labels with both thick and thin portions, the thin portions are prone to being lost during the erosion step of smoothing.
evidence: This describes a specific limitation of the erosion-based smoothing.

claim: The use of skeletonization and the edge-aware watershed allowed preservation of the core of thin portions in labels.
source: While a fully adaptive morphological approach would be beneficial, our use of skeletonization and the edge-aware watershed allowed us to preserve the core of such thin portions.
evidence: This describes how the authors addressed the thin structure preservation challenge.

claim: The combination of erosion, skeletonization, and watershed could serve as an adaptive form of morphological operations to better preserve any label's overall footprint and topological consistency.
source: More generally, the combination of erosion, skeletonization, and watershed could serve as an adaptive form of morphological operations to better preserve any label's overall footprint and topological consistency.
evidence: This is a generalization about the potential of the combined approach.

claim: More registration artifacts were observed with the whole-brain lightsheet microscopy images compared to the ADMBA images.
source: While the refined labels are superior to the original ones in both the ADMBA images and whole-brain lightsheet microscopy images, we observed more registration artifacts with the whole-brain lightsheet microscopy images (Figure 7A).
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in the validation results.

claim: Biological variation, the slight age mismatch (E18.5 in ADMBA vs. P0 for lightsheet), and different preparations and imaging modality are substantial factors contributing to registration artifacts.
source: Undoubtedly, biological variation, the slight age mismatch (E18.5 in ADMBA vs. P0 for lightsheet), and the different preparations and imaging modality (Nissl sections vs. nuclei-stained whole brain) are substantial factors.
evidence: This provides potential explanations for observed registration artifacts.

claim: Generating a group-wise composite of nuclei-stained whole brain could help reduce biological variation.
source: Generating a group-wise composite of nuclei-stained whole brain could help reduce biological variation.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future improvement.

claim: Deferring the edge-aware reannotation step until after registration, using boundaries identified in the nuclei-stained whole brain, may reduce registration artifacts.
source: Deferring the edge-aware reannotation step until after registration, using boundaries identified in the nuclei-stained whole brain, may also reduce these artifacts.
evidence: This is another suggestion for future improvement.

claim: Integrating anatomical edge maps with in-situ hybridization expression patterns may improve label boundaries.
source: Integrating our anatomical edge maps with in-situ hybridization expression patterns (Allen Institute for Brain Science, 2017; Thompson et al., 2014b) may similarly improve label boundaries.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future improvement based on integration with other data types.

claim: A deep learning model utilized histological textures to generate labels, requiring substantial manual annotation as initial ground truth.
source: A deep learning model utilized histological textures to generate labels (Chen et al., 2019). Training the model required substantial manual annotation to serve as the initial ground truth; in this context, our automated approach to atlases generation may be able to replace or augment this manual step.
evidence: This describes a related approach and suggests how the current work could complement it.

claim: Fractional differential operators could be incorporated into the 3D anatomical edge map generation step to further delineate labels at higher or even full resolution.
source: Another recent approach used fractional differential operators to preserve texture as well as edge information for segmentation of single-cell resolution data (Xu et al., 2019b). This could be incorporated into the 3D anatomical edge map generation step to further delineate labels at higher or even full resolution.
evidence: This describes another potential future improvement based on recent methods.

claim: Mouse whole-brain imaging has been used to understand models of human traits and disorders, including sexual dimorphism, Alzheimer's disease, serotonin dysregulation, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorder.
source: Mouse whole-brain imaging has been used to understand models of human traits, including sexual dimorphism (Kim et al., 2017) and models of human disorders, including Alzheimer's disease (Liebmann et al., 2016; Delafontaine-Martel et al., 2018; Whitesell et al., 2019), serotonin dysregulation (Ellegood et al., 2018), epilepsy (Intson et al., 2019), and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (Suetterlin et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes applications of whole-brain imaging, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Accurate 3D reference atlases would augment analyses of mouse models by allowing detection of subtle quantitative changes not readily appreciable in individual slices.
source: Such analyses would be augmented by accurate 3D reference atlases, allowing the detection of subtle quantitative changes not readily appreciable in individual slices.
evidence: This describes the potential impact of improved 3D atlases.

claim: The completed and refined 3D ADMBA serves as a resource to help identify biological differences in multiple models of human disorders and traits across brain development.
source: The completed and refined 3D ADMBA serves as a resource to help identify biological differences in the multiple models of human disorders and traits across brain development.
evidence: This describes the intended use and impact of the refined atlases.

claim: The MagellanMapper software suite consists of both a graphical user interface (GUI) for visualization and a command-line interface for automation.
source: To facilitate both automated atlas refinement and visual inspection of large 3D microscopy images, we developed the open-source MagellanMapper software suite. This Python-based (Oliphant, 2007; Millman and Aivazis, 2011) image processing software consists of both a graphical user interface (GUI) for visualization and a command-line interface for automation (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This describes the structure of the MagellanMapper software.

claim: A major goal of the MagellanMapper GUI is to enable unfiltered, raw visualization and annotation of original 2D images in a 3D context.
source: A major goal of the suite's GUI is to enable unfiltered, raw visualization and annotation of original 2D images in a 3D context.
evidence: This describes a design goal of the software.

claim: The MagellanMapper GUI consists of three main components: an ROI selector and 3D visualizer, a serial 2D ROI visualizer and annotator, and a simultaneous orthogonal plane viewer with atlas label editing tools.
source: The GUI consists of three main components: (1) A region of interest (ROI) selector and 3D visualizer with 3D rendering, (2) A serial 2D ROI visualizer and annotator, tailored for building truth sets of 3D nuclei positions, and (3) A simultaneous orthogonal plane viewer with atlas label editing tools, including painting designed for use with a pen and edge interpolation to smoothly fill in changes between two edited, non-adjacent planes.
evidence: This describes the components of the MagellanMapper GUI.

claim: The MagellanMapper command-line interface provides automated pipelines for processing of large (terabyte-scale) volumetric images, including 3D nuclei detection at full image resolution.
source: The command-line interface provides automated pipelines for processing of large (terabyte-scale) volumetric images, including 3D nuclei detection at full image resolution.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the command-line interface.

claim: The MagellanMapper suite makes extensive use of established computer vision libraries such as scikit-image, ITK, Matplotlib, Mayavi, Numpy, SciPy, Pandas, and scikit-learn.
source: The suite makes extensive use of established computer vision libraries such as scikit-image (van der Walt et al., 2014), ITK (Yoo et al., 2002) (via SimpleITK Lowekamp et al., 2013 and SimpleElastix Klein et al., 2010; Marstal et al., 2016), visualization toolkits such as Matplotlib (Hunter, 2007) and Mayavi (Ramachandran and Varoquaux, 2011), and statistical and machine learning libraries such as Numpy (van der Walt et al., 2011), SciPy (Virtanen et al., 2020), Pandas (McKinney, 2010), and scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the software dependencies of MagellanMapper.

claim: The cross-platform capabilities of Python allow the MagellanMapper suite to be available in Windows, MacOS, and Linux.
source: The cross-platform capabilities of Python allow the suite to be available in Windows, MacOS, and Linux.
evidence: This describes the platform compatibility of the software.

claim: The MagellanMapper suite API includes 3D image processing functions designed to be useful as library methods for other applications.
source: The suite API includes 3D image processing functions designed to be useful as library methods for other applications.
evidence: This describes the intended use of the software beyond the specific application.

claim: All procedures and animal care were approved and performed in accordance with institutional guidelines from the University of California, San Francisco Laboratory Animal Research Center (LARC).
source: All procedures and animal care were approved and performed in accordance with institutional guidelines from the University of California, San Francisco Laboratory Animal Research Center (LARC).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: All mouse strains were maintained on a C57BL/6J background.
source: All strains were maintained on a C57BL/6J background.
evidence: This describes the genetic background of the mice used.

claim: For timed pregnancies, noon on the day of the vaginal plug was counted as embryonic day 0.5.
source: For timed pregnancies, noon on the day of the vaginal plug was counted as embryonic day 0.5.
evidence: This describes the method for determining embryonic age.

claim: The size of the validation cohort (P0 wild-type mouse brains, n = 15) was chosen to detect an effect size of 1.5 after correction for multiple comparisons using a power calculation based on a paired t-test.
source: The size of our validation cohort (P0 wild-type mouse brains, n = 15) was chosen to detect an effect size of 1.5 after correction for multiple comparisons using a power calculation based on a paired t-test.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the sample size.

claim: Samples were cleared using the advanced CUBIC clearing protocol for whole-brain and whole-body clearing.
source: Samples were cleared using the advanced CUBIC clearing protocol for whole-brain and whole-body clearing (Susaki et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the tissue clearing method used.

claim: Samples were immersed in Reagent-1 containing 1 µM SYTO 16 for nuclear staining during the clearing process.
source: In short, samples were immersed in 1/2-water-diluted Reagent-1 containing 1 µM SYTO 16 (Thermo Fisher) and incubated at 37°C for 6 hr (Reagent-1: 25 weight% (w%) Urea, 25 wt% Quadrol, 15 wt% Triton X-100, and dH2O).
evidence: This describes the nuclear staining method used during clearing.

claim: Lightsheet imaging required approximately 50 tiles (5 × 10) per brain at 5x magnification.
source: Lightsheet imaging of a mouse P0 brain required approximately 50 tiles (5 × 10) per brain at 5x (Zeiss EC Plan-Neofluar 5x, NA 0.16, RI 1.45, WD 5.6 mm), which afforded a level of resolution that allowed for nuclei detection (0.913 µm/px lateral resolution).
evidence: This describes the imaging parameters used.

claim: The lateral resolution of lightsheet imaging at 5x was 0.913 µm/px.
source: Lightsheet imaging of a mouse P0 brain required approximately 50 tiles (5 × 10) per brain at 5x (Zeiss EC Plan-Neofluar 5x, NA 0.16, RI 1.45, WD 5.6 mm), which afforded a level of resolution that allowed for nuclei detection (0.913 µm/px lateral resolution).
evidence: This specifies the imaging resolution.

claim: A custom 3D-printed rod with a platform was designed to maximize surface area for gluing the ventral surface of the brain to the mount for lightsheet imaging.
source: To suspend the relatively larger whole brain, we designed a custom 3D-printed rod with a platform to maximize surface area for gluing the ventral surface of the brain to the mount (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a custom tool developed for the imaging process.

claim: The z-stack for lightsheet imaging typically ranged from 800–1000 planes using a slice interval of 4.935 µm with a lightsheet thickness of 10.44 µm.
source: We ranged the z-stack from just beyond the first and last z-planes with visible nuclei, typically 800–1000 planes using a slice interval of 4.935 µm with a lightsheet thickness of 10.44 µm, and set the image tiling to include the farthest lateral and anterior-posterior nuclei with a 10% overlap per tile.
evidence: This describes the z-stack parameters for imaging.

claim: The microscope paused for 20 s between each tile to allow tissue settling after repositioning for the next tile.
source: The microscope paused for 20 s between each tile to allow tissue settling after repositioning for the next tile.
evidence: This describes a technical detail of the imaging process.

claim: The BigStitcher plugin was used for image stitching, accessed headlessly through its scriptable interface.
source: To stitch the tiled microscopy images in an automated fashion, we used the Fiji/ImageJ (Schindelin et al., 2012; Rueden et al., 2017) BigStitcher plugin (Hörl et al., 2019), a successor to the Stitching plugin (Preibisch et al., 2009) that allows for better memory management and multiprocessing as well as a graphical interface to verify alignments. As we needed to stitch multiple brains, we accessed this plugin headlessly through its scriptable interface, manually intervening only to visually verify alignments before proceeding with the fusion step.
evidence: This describes the image stitching method used.

claim: The BigStitcher plugin auto-detected the brightest illuminator for each tile, discarding planes from the other illuminator.
source: After importing the CZI file into the BigStitcher HDF5-based format, the plugin auto-detected the brightest illuminator for each tile, discarding planes from the other illuminator.
evidence: This describes a feature of the stitching process.

claim: Tile shifts were calculated using a phase correlation method with links filtered below a correlation threshold of r = 0.8.
source: The plugin calculated tile shifts using a phase correlation method, and we filtered out links below a correlation threshold of r = 0.8 before applying shifts through the two-round iterative global optimization strategy.
evidence: This describes the tile alignment method.

claim: Approximately 10% of brains had tile misalignments that required manual repositioning.
source: To account for occasional tile misalignments, we manually inspected every pre-stitched brain to reposition any misaligned tiles, which occurred in approximately 10% of brains.
evidence: This quantifies the frequency of manual intervention needed.

claim: Images were subdivided into overlapping chunks to reduce RAM requirements and maximize parallel processing during nuclei detection.
source: To perform detections in large images several hundred gigabytes (GB) to over a terabyte (TB) in size, we subdivided the image into many smaller chunks to reduce RAM requirements and maximize parallel processing.
evidence: This describes the computational strategy for handling large images.

claim: The overlap size for image chunks was approximately the nucleus diameter to ensure nuclei at borders would not be missed.
source: We divided the image shape into overlapping chunks to ensure that nuclei at borders would not be missed, with overlap size of approximately the nucleus diameter.
evidence: This describes a parameter choice for the chunking strategy.

claim: Each chunk was further subdivided into sub-chunks for preprocessing based on its immediate surroundings to address local variation.
source: To address these issues, we analyzed images in a local manner by further subdividing each chunk for preprocessing based on its immediate surroundings.
evidence: This describes the preprocessing strategy to handle local image variation.

claim: In each sub-chunk, intensity values were clipped at the 5th and 98.5th percentiles to remove extreme outliers.
source: In each sub-chunk, we first clipped intensity values at the 5th and 98.5th percentiles (percentile in Numpy) to remove extreme outliers, rescaled the intensities from 0 to 1, and further saturated signal by clipping the rescaled intensities at the 50th percentile.
evidence: This describes a preprocessing step for nuclei detection.

claim: Unsharp masking with a Gaussian sigma of 8 was used to enhance edges during preprocessing.
source: We next enhanced edges by using unsharp masking with a Gaussian sigma of 8 (filters.gaussian in scikit-image) to identify sharp details as the difference between an image and its blurred version (which we amplified by a factor of 0.3) and adding back those details to the original image.
evidence: This describes an edge enhancement preprocessing step.

claim: The blob detector was set with a minimum and maximum sigma based on microscopy resolution, 10 intermediate values, detection threshold of 0.1, and overlap fraction threshold of 0.55.
source: We set the minimum and maximum sigma based on the microscopy resolution, with 10 intermediate values, detection threshold of 0.1, and overlap fraction threshold of 0.55 below which duplicated blobs are eliminated.
evidence: This describes the parameters for the blob detection algorithm.

claim: Images were interpolated in the z-direction to near isotropy before detection to improve detection along the z-axis.
source: To improve detection along the z-axis, we interpolated the images in this direction to near isotropy before detection (transform.resize in scikit-image).
evidence: This describes a preprocessing step to address anisotropy.

claim: Nuclei from the bottom and topmost z-planes in each ROI were cropped to avoid clustering and minimize duplication with adjacent ROIs.
source: The blob detector had a tendency to cluster detections in the bottom and topmost z-planes in each ROI from nuclei visible within the ROI but whose centroids are outside. To avoid this clustering and minimize duplication with adjacent ROIs, we cropped nuclei from these planes on the assumption that they would be captured better in the adjacent, overlapping ROIs.
evidence: This describes a post-processing step to handle edge effects.

claim: Duplicate blobs in overlapping chunks were pruned by finding blobs close to another blob within a given tolerance and replacing both with a new blob at the mean of their coordinates.
source: Within each overlapping region, we found all blobs close to another blob by taking the absolute value of the difference between all blobs with one another and finding blobs within a given tolerance in all dimensions. The tolerance was titrated so that the ratio of final blobs in overlapping regions to the next adjacent regions of same volume was about 1:1. For each close pair of blobs found, we replaced both blobs with a new blob that took the mean of their coordinates.
evidence: This describes the method for removing duplicate detections.

claim: Parameters for preprocessing, detections, and pruning steps were optimized through a Grid Search approach using truth sets of nuclei locations and radii.
source: Parameters for preprocessing, detections, and pruning steps were optimized through a Grid Search approach, a type of hyperparameter tuning, to check combinations of parameters systematically. To evaluate the accuracy of each set of parameters, two students in our lab generated truth sets of nuclei locations and radii using our serial 2D nuclei annotation tool, taking ROIs of size 42×42×32 pixels (x, y, z) from representative ROIs of all major brain structures (n = 15 forebrain, eight midbrain, and seven hindbrain; n = 2766 nuclei).
evidence: This describes the parameter optimization method.

claim: Truth sets contained n = 15 forebrain, eight midbrain, and seven hindbrain ROIs with n = 2766 nuclei total.
source: To evaluate the accuracy of each set of parameters, two students in our lab generated truth sets of nuclei locations and radii using our serial 2D nuclei annotation tool, taking ROIs of size 42×42×32 pixels (x, y, z) from representative ROIs of all major brain structures (n = 15 forebrain, eight midbrain, and seven hindbrain; n = 2766 nuclei).
evidence: This describes the composition of the truth sets.

claim: The Hungarian algorithm was used to determine optimal assignments between detected and ground truth nuclei.
source: After detecting nuclei on these images with a given set of parameters, matches between detections and ground truth was determined using the Hungarian algorithm, a combinatorial optimization method to determine optimal assignments between two sets (Kuhn, 1955), as implemented in optimize.linear_sum_assignment in Scipy.
evidence: This describes the method for matching detections to ground truth.

claim: True positives were taken as pairings within a given tolerance distance, while unpaired detections or those exceeding the threshold were considered false positives.
source: We took correctly identified detections, or true positives (TP), as pairings within a given tolerance distance. Unpaired detections or those in pairs exceeding this threshold were considered false positives (FP), and the same for ground truth were false negatives (FN).
evidence: This describes the criteria for evaluating detection accuracy.

claim: A two-stage search was performed to find pairings, first within an inner sub-ROI, then between unmatched inner sub-ROI objects and the rest of the ROI to avoid missed border matches.
source: Since a match for a given nucleus within the ROI may lie outside of it and thus go unseen, we first searched for pairings only within an inner sub-ROI, followed by a secondary search for pairings between only unmatched inner sub-ROI objects and the rest of the ROI (Ho et al., 2017). This approach reduced the total number of nuclei available (n = 1118 nuclei) but avoided missed border matches.
evidence: This describes a refinement to the matching process to handle edge effects.

claim: The final truth set used for evaluation contained n = 1118 nuclei after excluding border regions.
source: Since a match for a given nucleus within the ROI may lie outside of it and thus go unseen, we first searched for pairings only within an inner sub-ROI, followed by a secondary search for pairings between only unmatched inner sub-ROI objects and the rest of the ROI (Ho et al., 2017). This approach reduced the total number of nuclei available (n = 1118 nuclei) but avoided missed border matches.
evidence: This specifies the final size of the truth set.

claim: Image downsampling was necessary to reduce memory utilization during image registration.
source: As stitched images are typically several hundreds of GBs per file, image downsampling was necessary to reduce memory utilization during image registration.
evidence: This explains the rationale for downsampling.

claim: The target final size for downsampling was matched to the E18.5 atlas, which would be registered to each downsampled image.
source: We matched the target final size to the E18.5 atlas, which would be registered to each downsampled image.
evidence: This describes the downsampling target.

claim: Registration involved rigid followed by non-rigid alignment using SimpleElastix.
source: Registration involved rigid followed by non-rigid alignment.
evidence: This describes the registration strategy.

claim: Rigid registration employed a translation with 2048 iterations followed by an affine with 1024 iterations.
source: For rigid registration, we employed a translation (translation parameter map in SimpleElastix) with default settings except increasing to 2048 iterations (MaximumNumberOfIterations setting) followed by an affine (affine parameter map) with 1024 iterations, applied with an ElastixImageFilter, to shift, resize, and shear the atlas microscopy image to the same space as that of the sample brain.
evidence: This describes the rigid registration parameters.

claim: Non-rigid alignment employed a b-spline strategy guided by the AdvancedNormalizedCorrelation similarity metric with grid spacing of size 60 over 512 iterations.
source: For non-rigid alignment, we employed a b-spline strategy (bspline parameter map) guided by the AdvancedNormalizedCorrelation similarity metric (Nazib et al., 2018; Hammelrath et al., 2016) with grid spacing of size 60, measured in voxels rather than physical units (FinalGridSpacingInVoxels setting in place of FinalGridSpacingInPhysicalUnits), over 512 iterations.
evidence: This describes the non-rigid registration parameters.

claim: The final b-spline interpolation order was set to 0 for label images to avoid interpolating any new values and preserve the labels' specific set of integer values.
source: The TransformixImageFilter in SimpleElastix allowed us to apply the identical registration transformation to the atlas labels image, except that we set the final b-spline interpolation order (FinalBSplineInterpolationOrder) to 0 to avoid interpolating any new values, preserving the labels' specific set of integer values.
evidence: This describes a parameter choice to preserve label integrity during registration.

claim: The foreground of each atlas and sample microscopy image was taken to be its mean threshold for DSC calculation.
source: We took the foreground of each atlas and sample microscopy image to be its mean threshold (filters.threshold_mean function in scikit-image) and input them to a LabelOverlapMeasuresImageFilter to take the DSC.
evidence: This describes the method for calculating DSC.

claim: Volumes per label were measured by taking a mask of each registered label and summing the foreground pixels before multiplying by the microscopy pixel resolution.
source: We first measured volumes per label by taking a mask of each registered label and summing the foreground pixels within each mask before multiplying this volume by the microscopy pixel resolution (scaled for downsampling) to obtain volumes in physical units (mm3).
evidence: This describes the method for calculating label volumes.

claim: A nuclei heat map was constructed by converting nuclei coordinates to nuclei per voxel within the downsampled image.
source: For nuclei densities, we first constructed a nuclei heat map by converting the nuclei coordinates to nuclei per voxel within the downsampled image. We scaled the coordinates to the scaling of the downsampled image, rounding to the nearest integer, and found the counts of nuclei at each coordinate (unique with return_counts option in Numpy).
evidence: This describes the method for creating a nuclei density map.

claim: The 'elbow' point for determining the DBSCAN distance parameter E was found to be at least 20 µm.
source: To find E, the nearest-neighbor distance of the 2 · ndim − 1 neighbor for each point is sorted and plotted to find the distance at the 'elbow' point, the point of maximum curvature (Schubert et al., 2017), which we found to be at least 20 µm (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This describes the method for determining the DBSCAN distance parameter.

claim: The MagellanMapper suite is written in Python 3.6 with specific versions of libraries including Numpy 1.15, Scipy 1.1, scikit-image 0.14, and others.
source: The MagellanMapper suite is written in Python with the following versions and Python libraries: Python 3.6, Numpy 1.15, Scipy 1.1, scikit-image 0.14, scikit-learn 0.21, Matplotlib 3.0, Matplotlib ScaleBar 0.6, Mayavi 4.6, TraitsUI 6.0, PyQt 5.11, Python-Bioformats 1.1, Javabridge 1.0, SimpleElastix 1.1, and Pandas 0.23.
evidence: This provides technical details about the software implementation.

claim: Images were stitched with Fiji/ImageJ 1.52 using BigStitcher 0.2.10.
source: We stitched images with Fiji/ImageJ 1.52 using BigStitcher 0.2.10.
evidence: This provides technical details about the stitching software.

claim: Most software development was conducted on a Mid-2014 MacBook Pro with MacOS 10.13.
source: We conducted most software development on a Mid-2014 MacBook Pro (Intel Core i7-4980HQ, 16 GB RAM, 1TB SSD) with MacOS 10.13, image stitching and nuclei detections on AWS EC2 c5.9xlarge instances (36 vCPUs, 72 GB RAM, typically configured with 1TB SSD) running RHEL 7.5 and Ubuntu 18.04, and volume measurements and aggregation on a Dell Precision T7500 workstation (64 GB RAM, 256 GB SSD and 2.2TB HDD) with Ubuntu 18.04.
evidence: This provides details about the computational environment.
